claims.text: The starting W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is nanocrystalline.
The nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy is produced by spark plasma sintering.
Approximately 0.5 vol% Y2O3 nanoparticles can be incorporated uniformly into W38Ta36Cr15V11 through powder mixing and consolidation.
Adding approximately 0.5 vol% Y2O3 will suppress radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 600°C and 8 dpa.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will act as heterogeneous sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will capture migrating solute atoms.
Y2O3 nanoparticles will trap irradiation-generated vacancies and interstitials.
Defect and solute trapping by Y2O3 will reduce local supersaturations that drive radiation-induced precipitation.
Reduced local supersaturation will inhibit precipitate nucleation and growth.
The Y2O3 addition will preserve the nanocrystalline matrix during irradiation.
Preservation of the nanocrystalline matrix is critical for maintaining low irradiation hardening.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have more than 50% lower radiation-induced precipitate volume fraction than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have more than 50% lower radiation-induced precipitate density than the unmodified alloy.
Irradiation hardening in the Y2O3-modified alloy will be comparable to or slightly lower than in the unmodified alloy.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 undergoes significant radiation-induced precipitation under similar irradiation conditions.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening under similar irradiation conditions.
Spark plasma sintering can preserve the nanoscale grain structure after Y2O3 addition.
Avoiding prolonged high-temperature exposure will prevent unacceptable Y2O3 agglomeration.
Suppressing precipitation while retaining low hardening will enhance the alloy's microstructural and mechanical stability.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies a greater than 50% reduction in precipitate density and volume fraction, but the stated falsification threshold only rejects reductions below 30% and addresses density rather than both metrics. A 30–50% reduction would fail the quantitative prediction without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
